claim: Doa10 is a ubiquitin ligase in ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD).
source: The cytosolic ATPase Cdc48 drives extraction by pulling on polyubiquitinated substrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERAD and is cited in the introduction referencing prior work on Doa10 as a ubiquitin ligase.

claim: Doa10 is a retrotranslocase that facilitates membrane protein extraction.
source: Using a reconstituted system with purified proteins from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we show that the ubiquitin ligase Doa10 (Teb-4/MARCH6 in animals) is a retrotranslocase that facilitates membrane protein extraction.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, demonstrated through multiple experimental approaches including Get3 capture, antibody accessibility, and protease protection assays.

claim: A substrate's TM segment interacts with the membrane-embedded domain of Doa10.
source: A substrate's TM segment interacts with the membrane-embedded domain of Doa10 and then passively moves into the aqueous phase.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that the identity of the TM segment is important for retrotranslocation and ubiquitination (Figure 4, Figure 5).

claim: The substrate's TM segment passively moves into the aqueous phase after interacting with Doa10.
source: A substrate's TM segment interacts with the membrane-embedded domain of Doa10 and then passively moves into the aqueous phase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Get3 capture assay showing that chaperones alone can drive retrotranslocation without ATP hydrolysis (Figure 1C,D).

claim: Luminal substrate segments cross the membrane in an unfolded state.
source: Luminal substrate segments cross the membrane in an unfolded state.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with Ubc6-SBP bound to streptavidin, showing that the streptavidin-SBP interaction must be broken for retrotranslocation to occur (Figure 6).

claim: Unfolding of luminal segments occurs on the luminal side of the membrane by cytoplasmic Cdc48 action.
source: Their unfolding occurs on the luminal side of the membrane by cytoplasmic Cdc48 action.
evidence: This is shown by the experiment where Cdc48 acting on cytoplasmic polyubiquitin chains causes dissociation of streptavidin from the SBP-tag in the liposome lumen (Figure 6E,F).

claim: Cdc48 is a cytosolic ATPase that drives extraction by pulling on polyubiquitinated substrates.
source: The cytosolic ATPase Cdc48 drives extraction by pulling on polyubiquitinated substrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work (Bays et al., 2001; Garza et al., 2009; Jarosch et al., 2002; Nakatsukasa et al., 2008; Rabinovich et al., 2002; Ye et al., 2001).

claim: Hrd1 and Doa10 are two universally conserved membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligases that ubiquitinate ERAD substrates.
source: Studies in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae identified two universally conserved membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligases that ubiquitinate ERAD substrates, Hrd1 (SYVN1 in human) (Bordallo et al., 1998; Hampton et al., 1996; Kikkert et al., 2004; Nadav et al., 2003) and Doa10 (TEB-4/MARCH6 in animals, SUD-1 in Arabidopsis thaliana) (Doblas et al., 2013; Hassink et al., 2005; Swanson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies in yeast.

claim: Doa10 is a 150 kDa protein with 14 TM segments.
source: Doa10 is a 150 kDa protein with 14 TM segments (Kreft et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from prior structural characterization of Doa10.

claim: Doa10 substrates include single- and multi-spanning membrane proteins of the ER and inner nuclear membrane.
source: Its substrates include single- and multi-spanning membrane proteins of the ER and inner nuclear membrane, but also soluble proteins of the cyto- and nucleoplasm (Ravid et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from prior characterization of Doa10 substrates.

claim: No completely soluble, luminal substrates of Doa10 have been described.
source: No completely soluble, luminal substrates of Doa10 have been described.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Doa10 works in concert with two ubiquitin conjugating enzymes (E2), Ubc6 and Ubc7.
source: Doa10 works in concert with two ubiquitin conjugating enzymes (E2), the tail-anchored membrane protein Ubc6 and the soluble cytoplasmic protein Ubc7 (Swanson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from prior work on the Doa10 ubiquitination machinery.

claim: Ubc7 is anchored to the ER membrane by Cue1.
source: Ubc7 is anchored to the ER membrane by Cue1 (Biederer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Ubc6 initiates ubiquitin chains by transferring the first ubiquitin moiety.
source: Ubc6 initiates ubiquitin chains by transferring the first ubiquitin moiety, whereas Ubc7 extends ubiquitin chains with mainly lysine 48 linkage (Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work and confirmed by the ubiquitination experiments in this study (Figure 2).

claim: Ubc7 extends ubiquitin chains with mainly lysine 48 linkage.
source: Ubc6 initiates ubiquitin chains by transferring the first ubiquitin moiety, whereas Ubc7 extends ubiquitin chains with mainly lysine 48 linkage (Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work and confirmed by the ubiquitination experiments in this study (Figure 2).

claim: Ubc6 is itself an unstable protein and degraded in a Doa10-dependent manner.
source: Importantly, Ubc6 is itself an unstable protein and degraded in a Doa10-dependent manner (Swanson et al., 2001; Walter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from prior work and is the basis for using Ubc6 as a model substrate in this study.

claim: In the presence of Get3, 43 ± 4% Ubc6 was released from liposomes with co-reconstituted Doa10.
source: In the presence of Get3, 43 ± 4% Ubc6 was released from liposomes with co-reconstituted Doa10 (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Get3 capture assay shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: When co-reconstitution of Doa10 with Ubc6 was prevented, only 7–9% of Ubc6 were found in the soluble fraction.
source: When co-reconstitution of Doa10 with Ubc6 was prevented by inhibiting SNARE-mediated fusion or when Ubc6 liposomes were fused with liposomes lacking Doa10, only 7–9% of Ubc6 were found in the soluble fraction, representing the fraction of Ubc6 sticking to the outside of the liposome surface.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Get3 capture assay shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Nucleotide hydrolysis was not required for Ubc6 release by Get3.
source: Nucleotide hydrolysis was not required for Ubc6 release and an ATPase deficient mutant (Get3 D57N) behaved indistinguishably from wild-type (WT) Get3.
evidence: This is shown by comparing WT Get3 and Get3 D57N in the Get3 capture assay (Figure 1C,D).

claim: Doa10 allows for passive movement of its substrate Ubc6 out of the membrane.
source: This suggests that Doa10 allows for passive movement of its substrate Ubc6 out of the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Get3 without ATP hydrolysis can drive retrotranslocation.

claim: In the presence of Doa10, the luminally-encapsulated part of Ubc6 becomes accessible to the antibody over time.
source: However, in the presence of Doa10, the sudden decrease in fluorescence was followed by a slower decrease to about 10% of the original fluorescence signal within 30 min. Thus, in the presence of Doa10, the luminally-encapsulated part of Ubc6 becomes accessible to the antibody over time.
evidence: This is shown by the antibody accessibility assay in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Ubc6 and Doa10 need to reside in the same membrane for retrotranslocation to occur.
source: Ubc6 and Doa10 need to reside in the same membrane as we observed only minor quenching above background when we used a mutant SNARE that only supports liposome docking (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is shown by the antibody accessibility assay using a docked SNARE mutant (Figure 1E,F).

claim: Only in the presence of Doa10, Ulp1-cleaved, and thus right-side out Ubc6 was accessible to TEV cleavage over longer incubation times.
source: Strikingly, only in the presence of Doa10, Ulp1-cleaved, and thus right-side out Ubc6 was also accessible to TEV cleavage over longer incubation times, indicating retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is shown by the protease protection assay in Figure 1G,H.

claim: Retrotranslocation of Ubc6 by Doa10 is very efficient.
source: Comparison of the fraction of correctly oriented protein and the released fraction shows that retrotranslocation is very efficient in all three assays.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the results of the three different retrotranslocation assays (Get3 capture, antibody accessibility, protease protection).

claim: ATP synthase does not lead to Ubc6 retrotranslocation.
source: Under these conditions, only a minor fraction of Ubc6 becomes accessible to the antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D). We conclude that retrotranslocation of Ubc6 is not due to some non-specific perturbation of the membrane caused by any multipass TM protein.
evidence: This is shown by the antibody accessibility assay with ATP synthase as a control multipass membrane protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).

claim: Doa10 allows membrane-inserted and retrotranslocated soluble states of Ubc6 to exist in an equilibrium.
source: The observation that traps such as Get3 or the antibody are sufficient to drive retrotranslocation to completion suggests that Doa10 allows membrane-inserted and retrotranslocated soluble states of Ubc6 to exist in an equilibrium (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chaperones or antibodies alone can drive retrotranslocation to completion.

claim: In the absence of Get3 or the anti-A488 antibody, the membrane-embedded state of the substrate is energetically favored.
source: In the absence of Get3 or the anti-A488 antibody, the membrane-embedded state of the substrate is energetically favored.
evidence: This is inferred from the equilibrium model and the observation that traps are needed to drive retrotranslocation.

claim: Get3 or the anti-A488 antibody shift the equilibrium towards the soluble state by binding to retrotranslocated Ubc6.
source: Get3 or the anti-A488 antibody shift the equilibrium towards the soluble state by binding to retrotranslocated Ubc6.
evidence: This is inferred from the equilibrium model and the experimental results.

claim: In the cell, retrotranslocation requires Cdc48 activity.
source: In the cell, retrotranslocation requires Cdc48 activity (Garza et al., 2009; Nakatsukasa et al., 2008; Ye et al., 2001), suggesting that the pulling force generated by Cdc48 provides the directionality.
evidence: This is cited from prior work and provides context for the Cdc48 experiments.

claim: Degradation of Ubc6 requires its own E2 activity, the E2 Ubc7 and its adapter Cue1.
source: Degradation of Ubc6 requires its own E2 activity, the E2 Ubc7 and its adapter, the membrane-anchored Cue1 (Biederer et al., 1997; Swanson et al., 2001; Walter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from prior work and confirmed by the ubiquitination experiments in this study (Figure 2).

claim: In the absence of Ubc7 or Cue1, polyubiquitination of Ubc6 was abolished.
source: In the absence of Ubc7 or Cue1, polyubiquitination was abolished, and we observed ubiquitin adducts of lower molecular weight (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is shown by the ubiquitination assay in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Monoubiquitination of Ubc6 occurs in the absence of Doa10 but is enhanced in its presence.
source: Monoubiquitination also occurred in the absence of Doa10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), but was enhanced in its presence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown by the ubiquitination assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C,D.

claim: Kinetics of transfer of the first ubiquitin onto Ubc6 were independent of the presence of Ubc7/Cue1.
source: Kinetics of transfer of the first ubiquitin onto Ubc6 were independent of the presence of Ubc7/Cue1 (Figure 2C), suggesting that monoubiquitination is a prerequisite for Ubc7-dependent polyubiquitination.
evidence: This is shown by the ubiquitination kinetics in Figure 2C.

claim: Monoubiquitination is a prerequisite for Ubc7-dependent polyubiquitination.
source: Kinetics of transfer of the first ubiquitin onto Ubc6 were independent of the presence of Ubc7/Cue1 (Figure 2C), suggesting that monoubiquitination is a prerequisite for Ubc7-dependent polyubiquitination. This is indeed the case, as a catalytically inactive Ubc6 mutant (Ubc6C87A) was not ubiquitinated, but an N-terminal fusion of ubiquitin with inactive Ubc6 (Ub-Ubc6C87A) was a substrate for Ubc7-dependent polyubiquitination (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with Ubc6C87A and Ub-Ubc6C87A (Figure 2D,E).

claim: After active site loading of Ubc6 with ubiquitin, Doa10 catalyzes Ubc6-monoubiquitination, followed by Ubc7/Cue1-dependent polyubiquitination.
source: Together, these results establish that after active site loading of Ubc6 with ubiquitin, Doa10 catalyzes Ubc6-monoubiquitination, followed by Ubc7/Cue1-dependent polyubiquitination (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is the model derived from the ubiquitination experiments (Figure 2).

claim: The reconstituted system faithfully recapitulates the in vivo ubiquitination pathway for Ubc6.
source: These results agree with observations made in intact cells and with recombinant soluble fragments of Doa10 and Ubc6 (Walter et al., 2001; Weber et al., 2016). Furthermore, they indicate that our reconstituted system faithfully recapitulates the in vivo ubiquitination pathway for Ubc6.
evidence: This is inferred from the agreement between the reconstituted system results and prior in vivo and in vitro studies.

claim: Cdc48- and ubiquitination-dependent extraction of Ubc6 was observed.
source: We observed Cdc48- and ubiquitination-dependent extraction of Ubc6 (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is shown by the extraction assays in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Extraction efficiency was dependent on the length of ubiquitin chains, with five ubiquitin moieties being minimally required.
source: Extraction efficiency was dependent on the length of ubiquitin chains, with five ubiquitin moieties being minimally required (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis of extraction efficiency as a function of ubiquitin chain length (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).

claim: In the presence of Cdc48/UN, 45 ± 17% of Ubc6 molecules with more than five attached ubiquitin moieties were extracted.
source: In the presence of Cdc48/UN, 45 ± 17% of Ubc6 molecules with more than five attached ubiquitin moieties were extracted, compared to 15 ± 4% in the absence of the Cdc48 complex (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the extraction assay shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: No extraction above background was observed when either Cdc48 or Ufd1/Npl4 were omitted.
source: No extraction above this background was observed when either Cdc48 or Ufd1/Npl4 were omitted.
evidence: This is shown by the extraction assays in Figure 3A,C.

claim: ATP hydrolysis by the Cdc48 complex was necessary for extraction.
source: Furthermore, ATP hydrolysis by the Cdc48 complex was necessary, as Cdc48E588A was inactive.
evidence: This is shown by the extraction assays using the Cdc48E588A mutant (Figure 3A,C).

claim: Polyubiquitin chains were required for extraction because no extraction above background was found when ubiquitination was performed in the absence of Ubc7.
source: Polyubiquitin chains were required because we found no extraction above background when ubiquitination was performed in the absence of Ubc7 or less than five ubiquitins were attached (Figure 3A,C,D).
evidence: This is shown by the extraction assays in Figure 3A,C,D.

claim: The Cdc48 complex provides the driving force for the extraction of a polyubiquitinated membrane protein.
source: Together, these observations show that the Cdc48 complex provides the driving force for the extraction of a polyubiquitinated membrane protein.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the extraction experiments (Figure 3).

claim: Doa10-C (TM segments 3–14) behaved similarly to full-length Doa10 in retrotranslocation assays.
source: Doa10-C behaved similarly to full-length Doa10, whereas Doa10-N resulted in only minor quenching above background (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown by the antibody accessibility assay in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Doa10-N resulted in only minor quenching above background in retrotranslocation assays.
source: Doa10-C behaved similarly to full-length Doa10, whereas Doa10-N resulted in only minor quenching above background (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown by the antibody accessibility assay in Figure 4A,B.

claim: TM segments 3–14 in Doa10 are sufficient to mediate retrotranslocation of Ubc6.
source: These results show that TM segments 3–14 in Doa10 are sufficient to mediate retrotranslocation of Ubc6.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Doa10-C (Figure 4A,B,C).

claim: Only the Ubc6 TM, but not the Syb TM, was retrotranslocated by Doa10.
source: We only observed retrotranslocation of the Ubc6 TM, but not of the Syb TM (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is shown by the antibody accessibility assay with Ubc6/Syb chimeras (Figure 4D,E).

claim: The identity of the substrate's TM segment is important for retrotranslocation.
source: Thus, the identity of the substrate's TM segment is important for retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Ubc6/Syb chimeras (Figure 4D,E).

claim: Replacement of the Ubc6 TM with the TM of Syb mildly affected polyubiquitination.
source: Replacement of the Ubc6 TM with the TM of Syb mildly affected polyubiquitination as seen by the emergence of shorter ubiquitin chains in the case of the Syb TM (Figure 5A,B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown by the ubiquitination assays in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Doa10-dependent monoubiquitination of Ubc6SybTM was impaired.
source: Doa10-dependent monoubiquitination of Ubc6SybTM was impaired (Figure 5C,D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D), while E3-independent autoubiquitination of this mutant was unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is shown by the ubiquitination assays in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The Ubc6 TM anchor contributes to the efficient Doa10-dependent ubiquitination of Ubc6.
source: Thus, the Ubc6 TM anchor contributes to the efficient Doa10-dependent ubiquitination of Ubc6, indicating a more efficient recruitment to Doa10.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ubc6SybTM has impaired Doa10-dependent ubiquitination (Figure 5C,D).

claim: Ubc6 polyubiquitination by Doa10-N was less efficient compared to full-length Doa10.
source: Ubc6 polyubiquitination by Doa10-N was less efficient compared to full-length Doa10 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is shown by the ubiquitination assays in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Co-reconstitution of Doa10-N and Doa10-C together restored ubiquitination to WT levels.
source: This was not due to impaired E3 activity, because co-reconstitution of Doa10-N and Doa10-C together restored ubiquitination to WT levels.
evidence: This is shown by the ubiquitination assays in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The Doa10 region that includes TMs 3–14 plays a role in ubiquitination of Ubc6.
source: We conclude that the Doa10 region that includes TMs 3–14 plays a role in ubiquitination of Ubc6.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Doa10 truncations (Figure 5E,F).

claim: Both ubiquitination and retrotranslocation of Ubc6 are sensitive to changes in the membrane-embedded regions of Ubc6 and Doa10.
source: Both ubiquitination and retrotranslocation of Ubc6 are sensitive to changes in the membrane-embedded regions of Ubc6 and Doa10, indicating a specific interaction of Doa10 with the TM domain of Ubc6.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Ubc6 and Doa10 mutants (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: The TM domain of Doa10 recognizes substrates and thereby contributes to the specificity of substrate selection.
source: Our results show that the TM domain of Doa10 recognizes substrates and thereby contributes to the specificity of substrate selection.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments showing that the identity of the TM segment affects both ubiquitination and retrotranslocation.

claim: A protein-protein interaction on the luminal side of the membrane acts as an anchor and prevents retrotranslocation of Ubc6.
source: Together, this shows that a protein-protein interaction on the luminal side of the membrane, mimicking the presence of a folded domain, acts as an anchor and prevents retrotranslocation of Ubc6.
evidence: This is shown by the experiments with Ubc6-SBP bound to streptavidin (Figure 6A,B).

claim: Retrotranslocation of Ubc6-SBP occurred depending on polyubiquitination and Cdc48 activity.
source: Retrotranslocation occurred depending on polyubiquitination and Cdc48 activity (Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown by the antibody accessibility assay with Ubc6-SBP and Cdc48 (Figure 6C,D).

claim: Streptavidin remained encapsulated in liposomes in reactions where Ubc6-SBP was extracted.
source: Importantly, streptavidin remained encapsulated in liposomes in reactions where Ubc6-SBP was extracted (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is shown by the flotation assay after extraction (Figure 6E,F).

claim: Cdc48 action on the cytosolic side of the membrane leads to dissociation of streptavidin from the SBP-tag in the liposome lumen.
source: Thus, Cdc48 action on the cytosolic side of the membrane leads to dissociation of streptavidin from the SBP-tag in the liposome lumen.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that streptavidin remains in the lumen while Ubc6-SBP is extracted (Figure 6E,F).

claim: The dissociation of the SBP tag from streptavidin is interpreted as unfolding.
source: As this reaction entails the breaking of bonds that are comparable to the intramolecular interactions that keep a protein folded, we interpret the dissociation of the SBP tag from streptavidin as unfolding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the nature of the streptavidin-SBP interaction.

claim: Doa10 retrotranslocates a luminal protein segment in an unfolded state.
source: Our results thus show that Doa10 retrotranslocates a luminal protein segment in an unfolded state.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Ubc6-SBP and streptavidin (Figure 6).

claim: Cdc48, acting on cytoplasmic polyubiquitin chains, generates a mechanical force that results in luminal unfolding and drives retrotranslocation.
source: Cdc48, acting on cytoplasmic polyubiquitin chains, generates a mechanical force that results in luminal unfolding und drives retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Ubc6-SBP and streptavidin (Figure 6).

claim: The integrity of the membrane is maintained during the retrotranslocation process.
source: The integrity of the membrane is maintained in this process.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that streptavidin remains encapsulated in liposomes during extraction (Figure 6E,F).

claim: Doa10 contributes to overcoming the energetic barrier for membrane protein extraction.
source: Our results provide evidence that Doa10 contributes to overcoming the energetic barrier for membrane protein extraction.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental results.

claim: Passive movement of a tail-anchored membrane protein into the aqueous phase occurs in the presence of Doa10.
source: This is demonstrated by passive movement of a tail-anchored membrane protein into the aqueous phase in the presence of Doa10.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Get3 capture and antibody accessibility assays (Figure 1).

claim: In the absence of a folded luminal domain, factors such as Get3 or an antibody that trap the retrotranslocated state are sufficient to drive the reaction.
source: In the absence of a folded luminal domain, factors such as Get3 or an antibody that trap the retrotranslocated state are sufficient to drive the reaction, bypassing the requirement for ubiquitination and Cdc48.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Get3 capture and antibody accessibility assays (Figure 1).

claim: Once dissociated from streptavidin, a 57 amino acid long luminal protein segment that includes the SBP-tag is retrotranslocated by Doa10 without markedly affecting retrotranslocation kinetics.
source: We show that, once dissociated from streptavidin, a 57 amino acid long luminal protein segment that includes the SBP-tag is retrotranslocated by Doa10 without markedly affecting retrotranslocation kinetics.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments with Ubc6-SBP (Figure 6).

claim: Doa10 can accommodate less hydrophobic sequences in the retrotranslocation process.
source: Thus, Doa10 can also accommodate these less hydrophobic sequences in the retrotranslocation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the SBP-tag segment is retrotranslocated.

claim: Doa10 does not accommodate a folded domain during retrotranslocation.
source: Our data show that Doa10 does not accommodate a folded domain during retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments with Ubc6-SBP bound to streptavidin (Figure 6).

claim: Unfolding of polypeptide segments on the luminal side of the membrane is a direct consequence of Cdc48 acting on cytoplasmically attached polyubiquitin chains.
source: Instead, unfolding of polypeptide segments on the luminal side of the membrane is a direct consequence of Cdc48 acting on cytoplasmically attached polyubiquitin chains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments with Ubc6-SBP and streptavidin (Figure 6).

claim: Degradation of TM domain containing Doa10 substrates, including Ubc6, strictly depends on Cdc48, Ufd1 and Npl4.
source: Genetic and biochemical experiments in yeast showed that degradation of TM domain containing Doa10 substrates, including Ubc6, strictly depends on Cdc48, Ufd1 and Npl4 (Foresti et al., 2013; Habeck et al., 2015; Huyer et al., 2004; Neuber et al., 2005; Ravid et al., 2006; Ruggiano et al., 2016; Wang and Chang, 2003).
evidence: This is cited from prior work in yeast.

claim: Cdc48 is recruited to the Doa10-complex via Ubx2.
source: Studies showed that Cdc48 is recruited to the Doa10-complex via Ubx2 (Neuber et al., 2005; Schuberth and Buchberger, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Cdc48-recruitment requires either autoubiquitination of Doa10 or substrate ubiquitination.
source: This recruitment is dependent on the ubiquitination activity of Doa10, suggesting that Cdc48-recruitment requires either autoubiquitination of Doa10 or substrate ubiquitination.
evidence: This is inferred from prior work on Cdc48 recruitment.

claim: The Derlin Dfm1 is required for degradation of Ste6*.
source: Moreover, the Derlin Dfm1, which also interacts with Cdc48 through its carboxy-terminal SHP-box, has been shown to be required for degradation of Ste6* (Neal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: TM segments access a binding site in Doa10 through a lateral gate.
source: We speculate that TM segments access a binding site in Doa10 through a lateral gate.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of Doa10 action.

claim: Doa10 might promote delipidation of TM segments and breaking of helix-helix interactions in multi-spanning membrane proteins.
source: This might promote delipidation of TM segments and breaking of helix-helix interactions in multi-spanning membrane proteins.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of Doa10 action.

claim: Membrane-bound retrotranslocases generally contribute to AAA protein-driven extraction of membrane proteins.
source: We propose that membrane-bound retrotranslocases generally contribute to AAA protein-driven extraction of membrane proteins.
evidence: This is a general proposal based on the findings with Doa10 and comparison to other systems.

claim: SNARE-mediated co-reconstitution of Ubc6 and Doa10 was achieved by mixing two liposome populations.
source: Indeed, mixing of the two liposome sets led to SNARE-mediated co-reconstitution of Ubc6 and Doa10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown by the co-reconstitution experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Doa10 was reconstituted mostly in the correct orientation.
source: Protease protection experiments showed that Doa10 was reconstituted mostly in the correct orientation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown by the protease protection experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: For Ubc6, 45% was correctly oriented, another 45% wrong-side out oriented, and a minor fraction not properly membrane inserted.
source: For Ubc6, 45% was correctly oriented, another 45% wrong-side out oriented, and a minor fraction not properly membrane inserted (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, I to K).
evidence: This is shown by the protease protection experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, I to K.
